Hitherto

hith-er-TOO -- from Middle English hider ('to this place') + to. · adverb

Hear It

What It Means

Hitherto is up until this point in time.

The lab's hitherto unpublished data finally appeared in a journal this spring.

Worked Example

The hitherto quiet neighborhood suddenly found itself in the news after the abandoned lot was chosen as the site for a new stadium.

Notice that hitherto marks a clear before-and-after: quiet up until now, and then suddenly not. It always signals that whatever comes next is a change from how things had been up to this exact moment.

How Hitherto Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

previously

previously: at an earlier time than now

heretofore

heretofore: up until now, in formal or legal writing

Antonyms

henceforth

henceforth: from this point onward, into the future

hereafter

hereafter: from now on, in the time still to come

How Strong Is It? — previously → hitherto → heretofore

previously vs. hitherto

previously vs. hitherto: The building was previously used as a warehouse before it became apartments.

heretofore vs. hitherto

heretofore vs. hitherto: The two nations had heretofore never signed a single formal treaty.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hither-

root — hither-: to this place (Middle English)

suffix — -to

suffix — -to: up to, toward (English)

Put it together

Put it together: Hitherto combines the old word hither ('to this place') with to -- literally 'up to this point' -- so hitherto always marks the line between how things had been and whatever change comes right after it.

Use the root in a new word: hither

Use the root in a new word: hither: "Come hither," the old sign on the antique shop's door playfully read, "and see what treasures await."
